title: Ottawa Sets 90-Day Deadline for Atlantic Immigration Applicants With Job Changes
excerpt: New IRCC officer instructions end the old practice of parking Atlantic Immigration Program files on hold: applicants with employment changes now get a 90-day document deadline, and officers must refuse applications that miss it.
body:
• IRCC has set a strict 90-day deadline for Atlantic Immigration Program applicants who change jobs or whose employer changes ownership to submit updated documents — previously there was no deadline at all.
  • Officers will now issue a procedural fairness letter laying out the required documents, and must refuse the PR application if the 90-day window is missed.
  • The updated instructions spell out specific rules and document lists for three employment-change scenarios, ending the old practice of simply parking applications on hold.
  • Indian workers in Atlantic Canada — especially hospitality and service-sector employees in New Brunswick — face new pressure to track paperwork tightly if their job changes mid-process.

Ottawa has quietly hardened one of the most relied-upon immigration pathways to Atlantic Canada. New officer instructions from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC), published July 23, 2026 under the title "Atlantic Immigration Program (AIP): Other situations," impose a 90-day deadline on applicants whose employment situation changes after they apply — and give officers no choice but to refuse the application if the deadline passes.

From an open-ended pause to a hard clock

Until now, when an Atlantic Immigration Program applicant changed jobs, shifted roles with the same employer, or saw their employer change ownership, the officer handling the file had no fixed timetable. The practice was to put the application on hold until the missing documents arrived. That grace period is gone.

Under the revised instructions, the officer must send the applicant a procedural fairness letter advising them exactly which documents are required and that they have 90 days to deliver them. If the documents are not provided within that window, the officer is instructed to refuse the permanent residence application outright. The rules also specify a different, more detailed set of documents from applicants than was previously required.

Three scenarios, specific paperwork

The updated guidance sets out distinct rules for three scenarios: a change in ownership of the applicant's employer, the applicant changing roles at the same employer, and other material changes to the job offer underpinning the application. Each scenario carries its own document requirements, tightening the evidentiary standard at exactly the moment an applicant's situation is in flux.

The logic reflects how the program works. The Atlantic Immigration Program is employer-driven: a job offer from a designated employer in Newfoundland and Labrador, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia or New Brunswick is the anchor of the application, supported by a provincial endorsement. When that anchor shifts, Ottawa now wants fresh proof — fast — that the applicant still meets program conditions, rather than letting incomplete files linger.

"The new approach means applicants cannot simply change jobs without considering how the move affects their immigration file."

— CIC News, reporting on the updated IRCC instructions

What this means for applicants in practice

For a worker in the middle of a PR application, the change is practical, not theoretical. Consider a cook in Moncton who accepts a better role at a different restaurant, or a truck driver in Halifax whose employer is bought out. Previously the application would sit on hold while the worker sorted out fresh paperwork. Now the clock starts the moment the officer issues the procedural fairness letter: 90 days to assemble an updated job offer, employer letters, provincial endorsement documents and work-permit records, or the application is refused.

That makes documentation management a live part of the process. Applicants should keep employment contracts, updated job offers, employer letters, endorsement documents and all correspondence with immigration authorities in one place, and treat any job change as a trigger to notify their representative immediately.

A program tightening on two fronts

The federal tightening arrives just as Atlantic Canada is also reshaping the program locally. On September 14, New Brunswick removed its sector-wide restriction on AIP endorsement applications for the accommodation and food services sector (NAICS 72), reopening the pathway to most hospitality workers — though eight occupations remain restricted, workers outside Canada face limits, and the province warns that eligibility does not guarantee selection from its candidate pool. New Brunswick has also suspended applications for new AIP employer designations for 2026.

The two moves together sketch a program that is opening specific doors while policing the ones already open more strictly. The federal message is consistency: employment offers must remain genuine throughout processing, and incomplete applications will no longer wait indefinitely.

What applicants should do now

Anyone with an AIP application in flight should review their file if their job situation has changed since applying — and anyone contemplating a job change should weigh the immigration cost before resigning. The 90-day deadline is not extendable by default, and a refused application means starting the pathway again, with years of planning at stake.

"If the applicant does not provide the required documents within 90 days, the officer must refuse their PR application."

— IRCC officer instructions, "Atlantic Immigration Program (AIP): Other situations," published July 23, 2026

Immigration consultants are advising clients to avoid voluntary job changes while a PR application is pending, and to line up all supporting documents before a change becomes unavoidable. In a program built on the employer-employee link, that link is now under a stopwatch.
image_caption: Parliament Hill in Ottawa, with the Peace Tower flying the Canadian flag. Federal immigration instructions published July 23, 2026 set a 90-day deadline for Atlantic Immigration Program applicants who change jobs or whose employer changes ownership.
nri_angle: Thousands of Indian workers and international-student graduates in Atlantic Canada use the AIP for permanent residence; a job change mid-application now triggers a 90-day paper deadline that, if missed, means outright refusal.
